headline: Pandemic-era law passed unconstitutionally because of proxy voting, appeals court rules
author: Lauren Kaori Gurley

paragraphs.text: A federal appeals court on Friday ruled that the passage of a massive Biden-era funding bill was unconstitutional because of the way Congress relied on pandemic-era rules allowing lawmakers to vote by proxy, rather than in person.

The U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit said in a 9-8 decision that the passage of a $1.7 trillion government funding bill violated the Constitution because it allowed lawmakers to vote by proxy.

Proxy voting allowed lawmakers to vote on behalf of other lawmakers who were not in the chamber at the time, which was a common practice in Congress during the coronavirus pandemic. Republicans in Congress criticized proxy voting at the time but often used it.

“We further conclude that the Act’s passage was unconstitutional because the Quorum Clause does not allow proxies to be included when establishing a quorum,” wrote Circuit Court Judge Cory T. Wilson, a Trump appointee. “Members of Congress must be present for quorum purposes — as the Supreme Court expressly held over 125 years ago, and as Congress has done ever since the Founding. ‘Proxy presence’ does not count.”

The court was being asked to look at outgoing Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton’s request to uphold an injunction and stop the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act. The law requires employers to provide reasonable accommodations to pregnant workers, including access to water, more bathroom breaks and restrictions on heavy lifting. The appellate court’s decision on Friday reinforced an injunction on that ruling.

However, the appellate court’s decision smacking down proxy voting could open the door to legal challenges to multiple laws passed during the Biden administration, when the coronavirus was still rampant.

“BREAKING: proxy voting ruled to violate constitutional requirement of presence,” outgoing Rep. Chip Roy (R-Texas) wrote on X. Roy was in Congress at the time and opposed the spending measure. “Been proud to be fighting unconstitutional proxy voting. This is a good result. Want to be in Congress? Show up.”
The case is expected to be appealed to the Supreme Court.

The Pregnant Workers Fairness Act has been challenged since taking effect in 2023. Conservatives have criticized regulations crafted by the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission under the Biden administration that included worker protections for abortion and fertility treatments.

Before the passage of the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act, pregnant workers had some legal protections from the landmark Pregnancy Discrimination Act of 1978, which specified that they should be treated the same as those who are “similar in their ability or inability” to work.
But, workers with severe morning sickness and other serious conditions such as preeclampsia, a potentially life-threatening blood vessel disorder, had been denied pregnancy accommodations.
Advocacy groups for pregnant women decried the appellate court’s move on Friday.

“This decision effectively erases essential rights to pregnancy accommodations for workers across Texas, Louisiana, and Mississippi,” said Inimai Chettiar, president of A Better Balance, a group that led the push for the law’s passage.
Pregnant workers in those three states, which are covered by the 5th Circuit, are likely to lose protections because of the ruling, she said.
